notes.b: The Gaeltacht is the area where Irish is the community language, the language people use in everyday life. Its extent has shrunk as speakers have declined, and the decline began in the 1800s.
points: Census 1851 (a count of the whole population) was the first census to count Irish speakers. It found about 1.5 million Irish speakers, about 23% of the population, and Irish-speaking areas then covered much of the west and south.
The Great Famine (1845–49) and emigration (people leaving the country) hit the poor, western, Irish-speaking areas hardest, so the Irish-speaking population fell fastest where Irish was strongest.
National schools, set up in 1831, taught through English, so children learned to read and write in a language that was not their home language.
English became the language of law, trade, politics, the Church and emigration. Parents saw English as the route to work, so many chose not to pass Irish on to their children.
Census 1891 shows the result: about 680,000 Irish speakers, about 14% of the population, down from about 23% in 1851.
notes.tip: Remember that 1851 is the first census to count Irish speakers, so give no Irish-speaker figures for earlier years. Exams ask about changes in the Gaeltacht since 1850, so use the 1851 and 1891 figures as your evidence of decline.

notes.h: Revival and the first official Gaeltacht boundaries
notes.b: From the 1890s people tried to reverse the decline. The new state then gave the Gaeltacht its first official boundaries, and later redrew them.
points: The Gaelic League (Conradh na Gaeilge), a revival movement, founded in 1893 by Douglas Hyde and Eoin MacNeill, promoted the language, to stop its decline.
The new state's language policy made Irish compulsory in schools and required for some public jobs, so that the state itself supported the language.

Coimisiún na Gaeltachta (the commission set up to define the Gaeltacht) reported in 1926 and defined two types of Gaeltacht. Fíor-Ghaeltacht ('true' Gaeltacht): districts where 80% or more spoke Irish.
Breac-Ghaeltacht ('partly' Gaeltacht): districts with 25–79% Irish speakers. The 1926 definitions together covered a large area across many western and southern counties.

The Gaeltacht Areas Order 1956 (a government order, not a new law) shrank the official Gaeltacht to areas where Irish was still the community language, because Irish had weakened in the Breac-Ghaeltacht districts.
The Department of the Gaeltacht (Roinn na Gaeltachta) was set up in 1956. Gaeltarra Éireann, the Gaeltacht industry body, followed in 1957. Later small extensions were made by order.
notes.tip: The thresholds are 80% for Fíor-Ghaeltacht and 25% for Breac-Ghaeltacht. Do not mix them with the 67% figure, which comes from the 2007 study and not from 1926. Do not give a Gaeltacht land area or a 1926 population.

notes.b: Today's Gaeltacht lies in seven counties, and one of them, Meath, is an unusual case because its Gaeltacht was planned by the state.
points: Gaeltacht areas lie in seven counties: Donegal, Mayo, Galway, Kerry, Cork, Waterford and Meath.

The Meath Gaeltacht was built by planned colonies (settlements created by the state, not areas where Irish had survived): Ráth Chairn, settled in 1935 by families moved from Connemara, and Baile Ghib, settled in 1937.
Galway (Conamara) has the largest Gaeltacht population; Donegal is second.
Census 2022: the Gaeltacht population was about 106,000, and about 20,000 Gaeltacht residents speak Irish daily outside the education system, so only a minority use it as an everyday language.
Nationally (Census 2022): about 1.87 million people (about 40%) said they could speak Irish, but only about 72,000 spoke it daily outside the education system.
notes.tip: Exams use graphs and short questions on daily Irish speakers in Gaeltacht areas. Note the gap between people who say they can speak Irish and those who speak it daily outside education.

notes.h: State and community supports for Irish
notes.b: The state and communities have built institutions to protect Irish, from development agencies to broadcasting and official recognition.
points: Údarás na Gaeltachta, the Gaeltacht development authority, was set up in 1980 to replace Gaeltarra Éireann. It creates jobs so people can stay in the Gaeltacht. The Gaoth Dobhair (Gweedore) industrial estate in Co. Donegal is an example of Gaeltacht industry.
Raidió na Gaeltachta began broadcasting in 1972. TG4 (originally Teilifís na Gaeilge) launched on 31 October 1996. Both give Irish a presence in the media.
The Official Languages Act 2003 (amended 2021) gives Irish official status, which means public bodies must provide services in it.
Irish became an official EU language in 2007 and gained full working-language status on 1 January 2022.
The 20-Year Strategy for the Irish Language, a long-term state plan, covers 2010 to 2030.
Gaeltacht summer colleges give young people intensive immersion in Irish, so they use the language all day.
notes.tip: Learn the dates: Raidió na Gaeltachta 1972, Údarás 1980, TG4 1996, Act 2003, full EU working language 2022. They give precise points for a Gaeltacht answer.

notes.h: Gaeltacht Act 2012: boundaries defined by language
notes.b: The 2012 Act changed how the Gaeltacht is defined. Instead of a fixed map, boundaries now depend on how much Irish is actually spoken.
points: The Gaeltacht Act 2012 defined the Gaeltacht by language use rather than by a fixed map, so boundaries now depend on language use.
Gaeltacht Language Planning Areas: 26, so the Gaeltacht is now a set of planning units, each needing a language plan (a local plan to strengthen the use of Irish).
Gaeltacht Service Towns, and Irish Language Networks outside the Gaeltacht, extend Irish use beyond the core areas.
notes.tip: Give the contrast clearly: language use, not a map, now defines the Gaeltacht, and there are 26 Language Planning Areas.

notes.b: Even with these supports, the use of Irish as a daily language in the Gaeltacht has kept falling. A 2007 study set out how much daily use is needed to keep it alive.
points: The Comprehensive Linguistic Study of the Use of Irish in the Gaeltacht (2007) found that Irish is viable as a community language only where at least 67% of people speak it daily.
Its 2015 update warned that Irish could cease to be the community language in most Gaeltacht districts within about ten years.
In-migration of English speakers (people moving in from outside) weakens Irish, because English becomes the language of daily life in the area.
Suburban growth, such as Galway city's spread west, brings the Gaeltacht edge into contact with English-speaking suburbs.
Tourism, emigration of young people and English-language media add further pressure on Irish as the language of the community.
notes.tip: The 67% figure comes from the 2007 study, not from 1926. Do not mix it with the 80% and 25% thresholds.

notes.b: Responses target the pressures above, by keeping Irish speakers in the Gaeltacht and giving them reasons and ways to use the language.
points: Housing with language conditions, so that Irish speakers can afford to stay in Gaeltacht areas.
Jobs through Údarás na Gaeltachta and Gaeltacht industry, so that people do not have to leave to find work.
Irish-medium schooling (teaching through Irish) and preschools, so children learn the language early.
Language plans in each Language Planning Area.
Family supports for Irish-speaking households, and Irish-language media such as TG4 and Raidió na Gaeltachta.
notes.tip: Exams ask for one strategy to address decline in daily speakers. Pick one from this list and explain how it works.

notes.h: Belgium: a language border made official
notes.b: Belgium is a brief comparison from outside Ireland: a language boundary fixed in law. There is more on its present-day relations in the notes on the next part of this topic.
points: The language border between Dutch- and French-speaking areas was fixed by laws of 1962 and 1963, so the boundary between language regions became official.

The first state reform came in 1970. Belgium became a federal state in 1993 (power shared between central and regional governments), with Flanders, Wallonia and Brussels-Capital as its regions. Brussels is officially bilingual.
notes.tip: Belgium is one of the expected examples when exams ask how changes in boundaries over time impact on cultural groups.

notes.h: Dublin's suburban growth and the Greater Dublin Area
notes.b: Dublin's growth has spread from the city into the surrounding counties, creating a city region (a city and the area that depends on it).
points: Suburban expansion (new housing on the edge of the city) from the 1950s and 1960s led to the Advisory Regional Plan for Dublin (Myles Wright, 1967), which proposed new towns west of the city: Tallaght, Clondalkin, Lucan and Blanchardstown.
Ballymun, an example of high-rise housing: seven 15-storey tower blocks built 1966–69 and demolished between 2004 and 2015 under a regeneration plan (a plan to rebuild and improve a run-down area).
Census 2022: County Dublin had about 1.46 million people.
The Greater Dublin Area (Dublin, Meath, Kildare and Wicklow) had about 2.1 million people in Census 2022, about 40% of the State's population.
Commuter towns (towns whose residents travel to work in the city) in the surrounding counties, such as Navan, Drogheda, Naas and Newbridge.
notes.tip: Exams ask about urban growth and expansion of a city region, with Dublin as the example. Use the Myles Wright plan, Ballymun and the Census 2022 figures as named evidence.

notes.h: Dublin council structures and regional authorities
notes.b: As Dublin grew, the areas that govern it were redrawn several times, from adding townships to splitting the county council.
points: Rathmines and Pembroke townships were added to Dublin city in 1930, extending the city boundary.

Local Government (Dublin) Act 1993: from 1 January 1994, Dublin County Council was replaced by Fingal, South Dublin and Dún Laoghaire–Rathdown County Councils. The county had grown too large to govern as one unit, and local government needed to be closer to the people.
Dublin Corporation was renamed Dublin City Council in 2002 under the Local Government Act 2001.
Census 2022 populations of the four Dublin local authorities: Dublin City about 590,000; Fingal about 330,000; South Dublin about 300,000; Dún Laoghaire–Rathdown about 235,000.
The Dublin Regional Authority was set up in 1994.

The Local Government Reform Act 2014 replaced the regional authorities, including the Dublin Regional Authority, with three regional assemblies from 2015: Northern and Western; Eastern and Midland; Southern.
notes.tip: South Dublin is a county council area, so do not confuse it with Dublin South constituencies. Write Dún Laoghaire–Rathdown with an en dash. Exams ask about Dublin council structures, so give the 1994 split and the reason for it.

notes.h: Problems of an expanding city region and planning responses
notes.b: A growing city region brings problems, and the state has responded with planning, transport, regeneration and new forms of governance.
points: Problems: urban sprawl (a city spreading outwards over farmland), long commutes, congestion, housing costs, one-off housing (single houses built in the countryside) and dormitory growth (towns that people sleep in but work elsewhere).

The National Planning Framework (Project Ireland 2040), published in 2018, aims for half of future population growth in the five cities (Dublin, Cork, Limerick, Galway and Waterford) and to limit sprawl.
Transport: the M50 orbital motorway (a ring road around the city) was built in stages from 1990, the Luas light rail opened in 2004, and DART serves the suburbs by rail.
Regeneration: the IFSC (International Financial Services Centre) was set up in the Docklands in 1987; the Docklands and Ballymun are regeneration areas.
The Citizens' Assembly reported in 2023, recommending a directly elected mayor (a mayor chosen by voters, not by councillors) for Dublin.
Limerick elected Ireland's first directly elected mayor in June 2024, after a plebiscite (a public vote on one question) in 2019.
notes.tip: Only the 2023 recommendation for Dublin is checked. Do not say Dublin has a directly elected mayor or give a date for one. Limerick was the first.

notes.h: Other Irish boundary changes and economic regions
notes.b: Dublin is not the only place where boundaries moved. Other cities were extended or merged, and the EU divided Ireland into economic regions for funding.
points: Cork city boundary extended on 31 May 2019, taking in suburbs such as Ballincollig, Glanmire and Blarney from the county.
Limerick City and County Council and Waterford City and County Council were formed by merger in 2014.
From 1999/2000 Ireland was divided for EU purposes into two NUTS 2 regions (the EU's standard statistical regions): the Border, Midland and Western (BMW) region, and the Southern and Eastern region.
The BMW region kept Objective 1 (poorest-region) funding status for 2000–06, which meant it qualified for the highest level of EU support.
The economic regions were drawn for EU funding, so their boundaries follow economic need rather than language or identity.
notes.tip: Use the 1999/2000 NUTS 2 split and the three regional assemblies since 2015 as the Irish economic regions setting, to show regions redrawn for economic purposes.

notes.b: The European Union began as a way to make war between European states impossible, by tying their economies together after the Second World War.
points: Reasons: peace after two world wars; rebuilding after the war; coal and steel placed under shared control, so no state could secretly build up weapons; economic growth; the Cold War (the rivalry between the communist East and the capitalist West).
Schuman Declaration, 9 May 1950 (now Europe Day), proposed pooling coal and steel production.
The Treaty of Paris (1951) put the shared control of coal and steel into practice, because it set up the European Coal and Steel Community (ECSC).
The Treaty of Rome (1957, in force 1958) set up the European Economic Community (EEC) and Euratom (the European Atomic Energy Community).
The six founders ('the Six') were Belgium, France, West Germany, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands.
notes.tip: Be ready to name the reasons for integration, the Schuman Declaration, the ECSC, the Treaty of Rome and the six founders.

notes.b: Deepening means the members drew closer together, with more shared rules and institutions. Only the dates are given here; the issues each step raised come later.
points: Single European Act: 1986, in force 1987.
Single market (one market with free movement of goods, services, people and money, so trade between members is easier): from 1 January 1993.
Maastricht Treaty: signed 7 February 1992; in force 1 November 1993, creating the European Union.
Euro (the shared currency): launched 1 January 1999 for banks and electronic payments; notes and coins from 1 January 2002.
Lisbon Treaty: in force 1 December 2009.

notes.b: Widening means adding new member states. Each enlargement is listed by date, with the countries that joined.
points: 1973: Ireland, the UK and Denmark, the first enlargement. 1981: Greece. 1986: Spain and Portugal.
1990: East Germany joined through reunification with West Germany, not as a new member state.
1995: Austria, Finland and Sweden.
2004: ten countries joined: Cyprus, Czech Republic, Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, Poland, Slovakia and Slovenia.
2007: Bulgaria and Romania, not 2004. 2013: Croatia, the most recent member.
The UK left on 31 January 2020, so it is now a former member, leaving 27 members with about 450 million people (2024).
notes.tip: Short questions ask the year Romania and Bulgaria joined (2007, not 2004), how many joined in 2004 or 1995, the most recent member (Croatia), the year Ireland joined and which country left in 2020. Ireland joined with the UK and Denmark; do not add Norway.

notes.b: The end of communism in Eastern Europe made the biggest enlargement possible, and it changed the EU for both new and old members.
points: The Berlin Wall fell on 9 November 1989, opening the way for former communist states to seek EU membership.

Copenhagen criteria (1993), the conditions for joining: stable democracy, rule of law, human rights and protection of minorities; a working market economy able to cope with competition; and the ability to take on the obligations of membership.
Most of the 2004 entrants (such as Poland and Hungary), and both 2007 entrants, were former communist states, which is why the fall of communism led to this enlargement.
Effects on newer members: economic growth, EU funds and emigration (workers leaving for richer members).
Effects on older members: competition for jobs and investment, and migration from the newer members.
Croatia joined the Schengen area (the area of passport-free travel between member states) in 2023. Bulgaria and Romania joined it fully on 1 January 2025.
notes.tip: Eastern European expansion is a named setting in the syllabus, so link the fall of communism in 1989, the Copenhagen criteria, the 2004 and 2007 enlargements and the effects on newer and older members.

notes.b: Enlargement brought Ireland both opportunities and competition. Ireland opened its doors early in 2004, which shaped who came and what followed.
points: In 2004 Ireland, the UK and Sweden were the only existing members to give the new members' citizens immediate access to their labour markets.
Polish was the most common language other than English and Irish spoken at home in Census 2016 and Census 2022, showing the size of the Polish community.
Advantages: a larger market; a labour supply for the Celtic Tiger economy (Ireland's period of rapid growth); cultural diversity; export opportunities.

Disadvantages: competition for foreign direct investment (companies from abroad setting up factories and offices) from lower-cost states; less EU regional funding for Ireland; pressure on wages and services.
Example of investment competition: Dell announced in January 2009 that it would move its manufacturing from Limerick to Łódź, Poland, with the loss of about 1,900 jobs.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level exams ask for advantages and disadvantages of EU expansion for Ireland. Give the Dell move from Limerick to Poland as your example, and mention only reduced regional funding, not other EU funding effects.

notes.h: Future expansion: benefits to the EU and candidates
notes.b: Further expansion would affect both the EU and the countries waiting to join. The current candidate countries are named in a separate subsection.
points: Benefits of further expansion for the EU: a larger single market with more consumers, which means more trade, and greater stability on its borders.
Benefits for candidates: access to the single market and to EU funding, and, because they must meet the Copenhagen criteria, reforms to meet the Copenhagen criteria (the conditions for joining).
notes.tip: Map questions ask about EU members, former members and candidates. The former member is the UK.

notes.b: Partition of Ireland (dividing the island into two political units) redrew a political boundary across a single island. Its present-day effects, including the Good Friday Agreement and Brexit, are in the next subsection.
points: The Government of Ireland Act 1920 partitioned the island. Northern Ireland was established in 1921 with six of Ulster's nine counties, so Ulster itself was divided.
Cavan, Donegal and Monaghan went to the Irish Free State.
The Anglo-Irish Treaty was signed in December 1921.
Boundary Commission (1925), the body set up to review the border: its report was not published, and the border was left unchanged.
The border created a nationalist minority in the north (people who wanted a united Ireland) and a small Protestant minority in the south.
Impact: nationalists in Northern Ireland faced discrimination, which fuelled the civil rights movement from 1968 and then the Troubles (the conflict in Northern Ireland).
Communities, parishes and farms were divided by the border, so everyday life was cut across.
notes.tip: Exams ask how changes in boundaries over time impact on cultural groups, and expect partition of Ireland, Belgium and former Yugoslavia. Give the minorities created and the effects on communities.

notes.b: Yugoslavia was a multi-ethnic federal state that fell apart in the 1990s. Its break-up shows how new borders can leave cultural groups on the wrong side.
points: Yugoslavia was a multi-ethnic federal state. Its new borders followed the old internal republic lines, leaving Serb, Croat and Bosniak minorities on the 'wrong' side of them.
Slovenia and Croatia declared independence in 1991, breaking away from the federal state; Bosnia and Herzegovina followed in 1992.
War and ethnic cleansing (forcing a group out of an area by violence) followed in Bosnia and Herzegovina.
Srebrenica, July 1995: about 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed by Bosnian Serb forces.
The Dayton Agreement (1995) divided Bosnia and Herzegovina into two entities: the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska.
Montenegro became independent in 2006, a further split of the old state. Kosovo declared independence on 17 February 2008; Serbia does not recognise it.
notes.tip: Give the Srebrenica figure only as about 8,000, and give no total death toll for the Yugoslav wars. Do not use figures from model answers, such as the number of Serbs outside Serbia.

notes.b: After the Second World War, borders in central Europe were moved by the victorious powers, and millions of people moved with them.
points: In 1945 Poland's western border moved to the Oder–Neisse line. The USSR took Poland's eastern lands, so Poland shifted westward.
Millions of Germans were expelled westwards, and Poles were resettled from the east into the lands Germany had lost.
The Berlin Wall was built in 1961, dividing Germany and Berlin, so the city was split in two.
Germany was reunified on 3 October 1990, so the division ended, after the Berlin Wall fell in 1989.

notes.h: Break-up of the USSR and Czechoslovakia
notes.b: The collapse of communism also split two multi-national states. One split left minorities behind; the other was peaceful.
points: The USSR (the Soviet Union) broke up in 1991 into 15 independent states, such as Estonia and Latvia.
Ethnic Russians became minorities in newly independent states. In Estonia and Latvia they make up roughly a fifth to a quarter of the population.
Czechoslovakia split peacefully into the Czech Republic and Slovakia on 1 January 1993, the 'Velvet Divorce'.

notes.h: Cyprus: a divided island in the EU
notes.b: Cyprus is a divided island that is also an EU member, so a political boundary there has a direct effect on how EU law applies.
points: The Turkish invasion of July 1974 divided Cyprus between Greek Cypriots in the south and Turkish Cypriots in the north.
The UN buffer zone, the Green Line (a strip that keeps the two sides apart), runs through Nicosia.
The 'Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus' is recognised only by Turkey, so almost no other state accepts it.
2004 Annan Plan referendum: about 65% of Turkish Cypriots voted Yes, and about 76% of Greek Cypriots voted No.
Cyprus joined the EU in 2004, one of ten countries that year,, but EU law is suspended in the north, so the division continues inside the EU.

notes.b: A non-European example of a political boundary redrawn along religious lines.
points: Partition of India, August 1947: India and Pakistan (including East Pakistan, now Bangladesh) were created along religious lines.
Around 15 million people were displaced, and hundreds of thousands were killed in communal violence (violence between religious communities).

notes.h: General conclusions on boundaries and cultural groups
notes.b: The examples can be pulled together into three conclusions, which are useful for ending a 30-mark answer.
points: Boundaries drawn across cultural groups create minorities, displacement and conflict, as in Ireland, Yugoslavia and India.
Boundaries drawn around cultural groups, as in Belgium, can reduce conflict but can harden division.
Shared institutions, such as power-sharing and EU membership, can soften the effect of a border.
notes.tip: Use these conclusions to link your examples in a 30-mark answer on how boundary changes impact on cultural groups.

keyTerms.definition: The areas where Irish is the community language; since 2012 defined by language use.
Districts where 80% or more of people spoke Irish, as defined by the 1926 Commission.
Districts with 25–79% Irish speakers, as defined by the 1926 Commission.
One of the 26 areas under the Gaeltacht Act 2012, each needing a language plan.
The first Irish census to count Irish speakers, showing about 23% of the population spoke Irish.
The admission of new member states to the EU, as in 1973, 1981, 1986, 1995, 2004, 2007 and 2013.
The 1993 conditions a candidate must meet to join the EU: stable democracy, a working market economy and the ability to take on membership obligations.
Dublin, Meath, Kildare and Wicklow, a city region of about 2.1 million people in Census 2022.
A county, city or town council responsible for local government in its area.
EU funding status for the poorest regions, held by the Border, Midland and Western region for 2000–06.
The division of a territory into separate states, as with Ireland in 1921 and India in 1947.
One of the two constituent parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina under the Dayton Agreement.
A neutral strip between opposing forces, such as the Green Line through Nicosia.

factCards.term: Irish speakers 1851 to 1891, and why the language declined
factCards.definition: Census 1851: about 1.5 million Irish speakers (23%); 1891: about 680,000 (14%). Causes: the Famine (1845–49) and emigration hit poor western Irish-speaking areas hardest; national schools (1831) taught through English; English was the language of law, trade and emigration.

factCards.term: Gaeltacht boundaries: how they were drawn and redrawn, 1926 to 2012
factCards.definition: 1926: Coimisiún na Gaeltachta drew a large Gaeltacht across many western and southern counties. 1956: the Gaeltacht Areas Order shrank it to where Irish was still the community language. 2012: the Gaeltacht Act based it on language use, with 26 Language Planning Areas.

factCards.term: Supports for the Irish language and the Gaeltacht since 1893
factCards.definition: Gaelic League (1893, Douglas Hyde, Eoin MacNeill); Department of the Gaeltacht (1956); Údarás na Gaeltachta (1980), e.g. Gaoth Dobhair estate; Raidió na Gaeltachta (1972); TG4 (1996); Official Languages Act 2003; full EU working language (2022); 20-Year Strategy 2010–2030.

factCards.term: The Gaeltacht today: counties and Census 2022 figures
factCards.definition: Seven counties: Donegal, Mayo, Galway, Kerry, Cork, Waterford and Meath (colonies at Ráth Chairn, 1935, and Baile Ghib, 1937). Galway has the largest Gaeltacht population, then Donegal. Census 2022: about 106,000 people, about 20,000 speaking Irish daily outside education.

factCards.term: Continuing decline of Irish in the Gaeltacht: evidence and pressures
factCards.definition: The 2007 study found Irish survives as a community language only where 67% or more speak it daily; its 2015 update warned most districts could lose it within about ten years. Pressures: in-migrants who speak English, Galway's spread west, tourism, youth emigration.

factCards.term: Strategies to address the decline of Irish in the Gaeltacht
factCards.definition: Housing with language conditions; jobs through Údarás na Gaeltachta; Irish-medium schools and preschools; a language plan for each Language Planning Area; family supports and Irish-language media such as TG4 and Raidió na Gaeltachta.

factCards.term: Belgium: how a language boundary was made official
factCards.definition: The border between Dutch- and French-speaking areas was fixed by laws of 1962 and 1963. The first state reform came in 1970, and Belgium became a federal state in 1993, with three regions: Flanders, Wallonia and bilingual Brussels-Capital.

factCards.term: Dublin's urban growth and the Greater Dublin Area
factCards.definition: Myles Wright's plan (1967) proposed new towns at Tallaght, Clondalkin, Lucan and Blanchardstown. Ballymun's seven 15-storey towers (1966–69) were demolished 2004–2015. Census 2022: County Dublin about 1.46 million; Greater Dublin Area about 2.1 million (about 40%).

factCards.term: Dublin council structures: how and why they changed
factCards.definition: Rathmines and Pembroke were added to the city in 1930. On 1 January 1994 Dublin County Council was split into Fingal, South Dublin and Dún Laoghaire–Rathdown, because the county was too big to govern as one; Dublin Corporation became Dublin City Council in 2002.

factCards.term: Regional assemblies and other Irish boundary changes
factCards.definition: In 2015 the Dublin Regional Authority (1994) was replaced by the Eastern and Midland Regional Assembly, one of three (with Northern and Western, and Southern). Limerick and Waterford city and county councils merged (2014); Cork city took in Ballincollig, Glanmire and Blarney (31 May 2019).

factCards.term: Dublin city region: problems and planning responses
factCards.definition: Problems: sprawl, long commutes, congestion, housing costs, dormitory towns. Responses: National Planning Framework (2018), half of growth in five cities; M50 (from 1990), Luas (2004), DART; Docklands and Ballymun regeneration; a directly elected mayor recommended in 2023.

factCards.term: Origins of the EU: reasons and founding steps
factCards.definition: Reasons: peace after two world wars, rebuilding, shared control of coal and steel, growth, the Cold War. Schuman Declaration (9 May 1950); ECSC (1951); EEC and Euratom (Treaty of Rome, 1957). The Six: Belgium, France, West Germany, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands.

factCards.term: Deepening of the EU: key treaty and market dates
factCards.definition: Single European Act 1986; single market from 1 January 1993; Maastricht Treaty signed 7 February 1992, creating the EU (in force 1 November 1993); euro 1999, with notes and coins in 2002; Lisbon Treaty in force 1 December 2009.

factCards.term: EU enlargement, 1973 to 1995: who joined when
factCards.definition: 1973: Ireland, the UK and Denmark. 1981: Greece. 1986: Spain and Portugal. 1990: East Germany, through German reunification. 1995: Austria, Finland and Sweden.

factCards.term: EU enlargement since 2004: who joined, and who left
factCards.definition: 2004: Cyprus, Czech Republic, Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, Poland, Slovakia and Slovenia. 2007: Bulgaria and Romania. 2013: Croatia, the most recent member. The UK left on 31 January 2020, leaving 27 members.

factCards.term: Eastern European expansion: background and effects
factCards.definition: After the Berlin Wall fell (9 November 1989), ex-communist states sought entry under the Copenhagen criteria (1993); most 2004 entrants and both 2007 entrants were ex-communist. New members gained growth and EU funds but lost emigrants; older members faced competition.

factCards.term: Impact of EU enlargement on Ireland: advantages and disadvantages
factCards.definition: Advantages: a larger market; workers for the Celtic Tiger (Ireland opened its labour market at once in 2004); diversity, with Polish the main other home language. Disadvantages: competition for FDI (Dell to Łódź, 2009); less EU regional funding; pressure on services.

factCards.term: Benefits of further EU expansion
factCards.definition: For the EU: a larger single market with more consumers, and greater stability on its borders. For candidate countries: access to the single market and EU funding, and reforms to meet the Copenhagen criteria.

factCards.term: Partition of Ireland: how the border was drawn
factCards.definition: The Government of Ireland Act 1920 partitioned the island; Northern Ireland (1921) took six of Ulster's nine counties, leaving Cavan, Donegal and Monaghan to the Free State. The Anglo-Irish Treaty followed (1921); the Boundary Commission (1925) left the border unchanged.

factCards.term: Partition of Ireland: impact on cultural groups
factCards.definition: It left a nationalist minority in the north and a small Protestant minority in the south. Discrimination against northern nationalists fuelled the civil rights movement (1968) and the Troubles (over 3,500 killed); the border divided communities, parishes and farms.

factCards.term: Break-up of Yugoslavia: boundary changes and impact on cultural groups
factCards.definition: Borders followed old republic lines, so the independence of Slovenia and Croatia (1991) and Bosnia and Herzegovina (1992) stranded Serb, Croat and Bosniak minorities. War and ethnic cleansing followed: Srebrenica (July 1995, about 8,000 killed); Dayton (1995) split Bosnia in two.

factCards.term: Post-war Poland and Germany: boundary changes and their impact
factCards.definition: In 1945 Poland's western border moved to the Oder–Neisse line and the USSR took its eastern lands; millions of Germans were expelled westwards and Poles resettled from the east. Germany was divided (Berlin Wall 1961–1989) and reunified on 3 October 1990.

factCards.term: Break-up of the USSR and Czechoslovakia: impact on cultural groups
factCards.definition: The USSR split into 15 states in 1991, leaving ethnic Russians as minorities, about a fifth to a quarter of the people in Estonia and Latvia. Czechoslovakia split peacefully into the Czech Republic and Slovakia on 1 January 1993: the Velvet Divorce.

factCards.term: Cyprus: a divided island inside the EU
factCards.definition: Divided since the Turkish invasion of July 1974, with the UN Green Line through Nicosia; only Turkey recognises the north. In the 2004 Annan Plan vote about 65% of Turkish Cypriots said Yes, 76% of Greek Cypriots No. Cyprus joined the EU in 2004; EU law is suspended in the north.

factCards.term: Partition of India, 1947: impact on cultural groups
factCards.definition: In August 1947 India and Pakistan (including East Pakistan, now Bangladesh) were created along religious lines; around 15 million people were displaced and hundreds of thousands were killed in communal violence.

questions.prompt: Changes in political boundaries can impact on cultural groups. Examine this statement with reference to examples you have studied.
questions.model: Partition of Ireland: the Government of Ireland Act (1920) and Northern Ireland's creation in 1921 with six of Ulster's nine counties left a nationalist minority in the north and a small Protestant minority in the south. The Boundary Commission (1925) left the border unchanged. Nationalists faced discrimination, which fuelled the civil rights movement from 1968 and then the Troubles. Communities, parishes and farms were divided. Break-up of Yugoslavia: a multi-ethnic federal state whose new borders followed its internal republic lines, leaving Serb, Croat and Bosniak minorities on the wrong side. Slovenia and Croatia declared independence in 1991 and Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992. War and ethnic cleansing followed, including the killing of about 8,000 Bosniak men and boys at Srebrenica in July 1995. The Dayton Agreement (1995) divided Bosnia into two entities. Montenegro became independent in 2006 and Kosovo in 2008. Conclusion: boundaries drawn across cultural groups create minorities, displacement and conflict; boundaries drawn around groups, as in Belgium, can reduce conflict but harden division; shared institutions can soften a border's effect.

questions.prompt: Examine how the boundaries and extent of the Gaeltacht have changed since 1850.
questions.model: Decline after 1850: the Great Famine (1845–49) and emigration hit the poor western Irish-speaking areas hardest; national schools taught through English from 1831; English became the language of law, trade and emigration. Census 1851 counted about 1.5 million Irish speakers (about 23%); Census 1891 about 680,000 (about 14%). Revival: the Gaelic League (1893). Official boundaries: the 1926 Commission defined Fíor-Ghaeltacht (80% or more speakers) and Breac-Ghaeltacht (25–79%), covering a large area across many western and southern counties. The Gaeltacht Areas Order 1956 shrank the official Gaeltacht to areas where Irish was still the community language, and the Department of the Gaeltacht was set up that year. Today the Gaeltacht lies in seven counties, with planned Meath colonies settled in 1935 and 1937; Census 2022 recorded about 106,000 Gaeltacht residents, of whom about 20,000 speak Irish daily outside education. The Gaeltacht Act 2012 replaced map-based areas with 26 Language Planning Areas, Gaeltacht Service Towns and Irish Language Networks, so boundaries now depend on language use. The 2007 study found Irish viable as a community language only where at least 67% speak it daily, and its 2015 update warned of decline within about ten years. Pressures include in-migration, suburban growth, tourism, emigration of young people and English-language media. Strategies include language housing conditions, jobs through Údarás na Gaeltachta, Irish-medium schooling and language plans.

questions.prompt: (i) Name two countries that have joined the EU since Ireland joined in 1973. (ii) Explain the advantages of EU expansion for Ireland. (iii) Explain the disadvantages.
questions.model: (i) Any two of: Greece (1981), Spain and Portugal (1986), Austria, Finland and Sweden (1995), Poland, Hungary and the other 2004 entrants, Bulgaria and Romania (2007), Croatia (2013). (ii) Advantages: a larger market for Irish exports and more export opportunities; a labour supply that helped sustain the Celtic Tiger economy; cultural diversity from new members' citizens, such as the Polish community, which is the largest after English and Irish at home (Census 2016 and 2022). Ireland, the UK and Sweden gave the 2004 entrants immediate access to their labour markets. (iii) Disadvantages: competition for foreign direct investment from lower-cost states, as when Dell moved its manufacturing from Limerick to Łódź, Poland, in 2009 with the loss of about 1,900 jobs; less EU regional funding for Ireland; pressure on wages and services as workers arrive from the newer members.
